metric.why: Transformer and switchgear lead times stretched from months to years and now gate construction schedules as hard as permits do. Lead-time surveys are published by industry groups and research firms; watch the directory sources.
metric.definition: Order-to-delivery time for transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators.

reading.body:
Long lead times for transformers and switchgear have become as hard a constraint on data center construction as permits, meaning a signed contract and approved site can still sit idle for years waiting for electrical equipment.

The equipment categories tracked here span transformers, switchgear, generators, cooling plant, and high-end accelerators. What they share is that each sits on a critical path: no substitution is possible, and delay in any one of them delays the building. When lead times stretch from months to years, the constraint shifts upstream from construction crews and concrete to factories and order queues that the data center operator does not control.

For AI specifically, this matters because accelerator clusters require dense, high-voltage power distribution, and that distribution depends on the same transformer and switchgear supply chains that are already strained by broader grid investment. A facility cannot commission GPUs until the electrical infrastructure is in place, so equipment lead times translate directly into delayed compute availability.

The data here identifies the metric and explains why it matters, but does not supply current lead-time figures. Actual order-to-delivery numbers are held by industry groups and research firms, and the definition notes that those sources should be watched directly. The sibling metrics on capital expenditure and colocation rental rates address cost, but neither covers this supply-chain timing dimension.
